roadmap.goal: Ship slice 06a of ADO Epic #5775 (Story #5791): an administrator opening the encryption panel understands what it is about, is offered only actions that would change something, and reads numbers that mean something. Eleven walkthrough findings, and they are one decision made twice — which actions exist and what the sentences say. Suppressing the move where it cannot help is also a rewrite of the warning that recommends it; hiding keys nothing references is also what stops the ring table needing an explanation. The four calls that are taste rather than derivation were taken by the maintainer before this wave and are recorded in the slice brief: the shortened startup custody line, the warning's wording, the panel header, and the rule that the emphasised button is whatever this instance's open problem is.
roadmap.overview: Six phases, 7 steps, back to front: the backend learns which keys anything was actually written under and stops implying it keeps a key it does not, then the panel loses the actions that cannot help, then the sentences stop counting nothing and stop guessing at plurals, then the screen says what it is for. The last step is documentation and the slice close.

slice_to_phase._not_in_this_roadmap_: removing keys from the ring — this hides only, and explicit removal is a later action that depends on slice 05b; the material comparison behind the published-key count (slice 04b, shipped); the docs pages and the Docker install (slice 06, #5781); the system information custody row and the emergency-admin field (slice 06b).

phases.name: Which keys anything was written under
phases.description: Every ring carries the published key as a read-only entry, so a first install appears to hold a key named after a legacy it never had, and a rotated one fills with chips that never encrypted anything. The answer is a query, not a decrypt: the key id is already written on the front of every stored value, so reading it any other way buys nothing — and it keeps the table renderable on an instance that cannot read its own secrets, which is exactly whose administrator is looking at this screen.

steps.name: Ask the database which keys its stored values name
steps.description: RED: create `ReferencedKeyIdsTests.cs` against real SQLite, seeded the way `PublishedKeySecretCountTests` seeds. Cases: values under one key report that id; values under two report both, once each; a value in the format this version replaced reports no id, because it carries none; an empty or absent value reports nothing; a value that is not a secret is not consulted; both OAuth token columns are consulted as well as connection options; an instance with nothing stored reports an empty set. GREEN: add `IReferencedKeyIds` with one method, implemented over `LighthouseAppContext` by selecting the stored values that carry an envelope and taking the key id off the front. Then narrow `EncryptionStateDto.KeyIds` to the active key plus the retired keys that appear in that set, leaving `EncryptionKeyRing` untouched. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): list the keys something was written under, not every key held`.
red_to_green_tests: Values under one key report that key id
Values under two keys report both, once each
A value in the format this version replaced reports no id
An empty or absent value reports nothing
A value that was never a secret is not consulted
Both OAuth token columns are consulted
An instance with nothing stored reports nothing
criteria: The ring is unchanged — a hidden key is still read with, and a restore brings it back into view on its own.
Nothing is decrypted to draw a table.
The key in force is listed even when nothing is stored under it.

phases.name: Where the key actually came from
phases.description: Under configuration custody the panel says `Kept in …/keys`, and that directory exists and is full of key-shaped files — the Data Protection key and the OAuth state secret both live there. An operator who backs it up alongside the database has every reason to believe they took their encryption key with them. They did not, and restoring that pair onto a host without the environment variable yields a database nobody can open.

steps.name: Name the setting where Lighthouse keeps no key, and shorten the startup line
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionControllerTests.cs` — the payload names the setting the key arrived in under each supplied custody, and names none where Lighthouse made the key itself; the pinned payload key-set gains exactly one name. Extend `StartupBannerEncryptionKeyLineTest.cs` for the shortened line: one custody word then the key store, no key id, across all four custodies. GREEN: carry the source name on the ring resolution the way `AnsweredByTheRetiredName` is already carried, expose it on `EncryptionStateDto`, and shorten `WhereTheKeyCameFrom` to the single words agreed in the slice brief. COMMIT: `fix(encryption): stop naming a directory the key is not kept in`.
red_to_green_tests: The payload names the setting a supplied key arrived in
The payload names no setting where Lighthouse made the key
The pinned payload key-set gains exactly one name
The startup line says one custody word then the key store
The startup line carries no key id
All four custodies read differently from one another
criteria: No row invites an operator to back up a directory that does not hold their key.
The banner still tells the four custodies apart by wording alone.

phases.name: One action, and the emphasis that follows the problem
phases.description: The move is offered unconditionally, offered twice at once under two names, and the only emphasised control is Rotate — which mints another key and is not what an upgraded instance needs. Worst is the instance whose key in force IS the published key: there the move re-encrypts that key onto itself, changes nothing, and leaves the warning standing.

steps.name: Offer the action this instance needs, once
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionPanel.test.tsx` across the states in the slice brief's table. Cases: nothing to move and no move offered; the key in force is the published key and no move is offered, with the custody sentence carrying the remedy instead; the alert names the action rather than carrying a button; no two controls call the same service method; the emphasised control is the move where something is on the published key, nothing is emphasised on a healthy instance, and Rotate is absent where the instance cannot mint. GREEN: drive both the presence and the emphasis of each button from the state already on `EncryptionKeyState`, and drop the alert's action slot. COMMIT: `fix(encryption): offer the one action this instance needs, and emphasise it`.
red_to_green_tests: Nothing to move, so no move is offered
The key in force is the published key, so no move is offered
The alert names the action instead of carrying its own button
No two controls do the same thing
The move is emphasised where something is on the published key
Nothing is emphasised on a healthy instance
Rotate is absent where the instance cannot make a key
criteria: Removing the alert's button also removes the three-line wrap it rendered as.
Every state in the slice brief's table is covered by a test.

phases.name: Numbers that mean something
phases.description: A count of zero is not information — it is four categories of nothing competing with the one number that matters. And both summaries interpolate a count into a hardcoded plural, as does the warning, which is the one sentence an upgrading operator is most likely to read.

steps.name: Say only what is not zero, in the grammar the count deserves
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionPanel.test.tsx`. Cases: a check on a healthy instance names only the state that has secrets in it; a check across several states names each non-zero one with its count and no zeros; one secret reads in the singular everywhere including the warning; a rotation with nothing stored says a key was made and mentions no move; a rotation that moved something says both; an unreadable secret is named however few there are. GREEN: replace `summaryOf` with an assembly that collects only the non-empty categories and pluralises off the count, and give rotation its own sentence. COMMIT: `fix(encryption): stop counting nothing, and agree in number`.
red_to_green_tests: A healthy check names one state and no zeros
A mixed check names every non-zero state with its count
One secret reads in the singular, in both summaries and the warning
A rotation with nothing stored says a key was made
A rotation that moved something says both
An unreadable secret is named however few there are
criteria: No sentence on this panel can render the word zero.
An unreadable secret is never hidden by the rule that hides empty categories.

phases.name: Saying what the screen is about
phases.description: Read cold, the panel opens on a table whose first row is Key source, with nothing establishing the subject. And the rotation instruction names a setting the operator did not set, differing from theirs by one character, with a grammar that is never given — the only rotation procedure this population is ever handed.

steps.name: A header, and a warning that leads with the situation
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionPanel.test.tsx` — the header establishes the subject and links onward before any table row is read; the warning states the situation, then the action, and carries no explanation of why the published key is bad; nothing rendered anywhere on the panel is key material in any encoding or a stored credential. GREEN: add the header and link agreed in the slice brief, and rewrite the warning to the wording agreed there. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): say what the encryption panel is about`.
red_to_green_tests: The header establishes the subject before the table
The header links to the documentation
The warning states the situation and then the action
The warning does not explain why that key is bad
Nothing on the panel is key material or a credential
criteria: The header is one line; the docs carry the teaching.
The link points at the page slice 06 will own, so it does not have to be moved later.

steps.name: A rotation instruction somebody can follow
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionPanel.test.tsx` for operator-owned custody. Cases: the instruction names the setting the operator actually set rather than the one differing by a character; it says both spellings exist and which wins; it gives the ring grammar — comma-separated entries, each bare base64 or name-colon-base64 — and says the first entry is the one in force; it says what to do with the setting they were using before; it links onward. GREEN: rewrite the instruction against `KeyRingSerializer`'s actual grammar. This is also the sentence every Kubernetes operator reads once the chart lands, so it is written to serve both. COMMIT: `fix(encryption): give a rotation instruction that can be followed`.
red_to_green_tests: The instruction names the setting the operator set
It says both spellings exist and which one wins
It gives the separator and the entry grammar
It says which entry becomes the key in force
It says what to do with the previous setting
criteria: Every token an operator has to type appears in the instruction.
The same sentence serves a Kubernetes operator without being written twice.

phases.name: Documentation and slice close
phases.description: The panel now names settings and a grammar, and the documentation has to agree with it word for word or the next operator reads two different instructions.

steps.name: Give the panel a page, and make the two say the same thing
steps.description: Write `docs/settings/encryption.md` following the shape every other settings tab already uses - `parent: System Settings`, a screenshot in `assets/settings/`, prose describing what the screen shows and what checking, moving and rotating each do. This is the page the panel's Read more link points at, which is why it ships in this slice rather than in slice 06. Then update `docs/Installation/configuration.md` so the ring grammar, the two setting names and which one wins read the same as the panel, and link the two pages to each other rather than repeating either. Regenerate the panel screenshot through the `@screenshot` run, removing the old image first so a sub-threshold diff cannot keep it. Record the slice verdict, and mark F-2, F-3, F-4, F-5, F-7, F-8, F-9, F-10, F-11, F-12, F-14, F-15 and F-18 addressed in `verification/manual-walkthrough.md`. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): give the encryption panel a page of its own`.
criteria: The panel's link resolves to a page that exists, in this same slice.
The grammar in the docs and the grammar on the panel are the same sentence.
The screenshot shows the panel this slice produces, not the one it replaced.
No internal reference numbers appear in prose a user reads.
